put_down.why: She came for how to start a company. Both company chapters (22 and 37) are placeholders, and the hands-on pricing chapter repeats chapter 19, which she had already read, so she stops.

buy_at_put_down.format: none yet; ebook if the company chapters were written
buy_at_put_down.would_pay: nothing now; about £9.99 for the ebook once ch 22 and 37 are real
buy_at_put_down.why: I came to learn how to start a company, and the two chapters that do it are placeholders. The pricing chapter then repeated one I had read.

interview: It is a book that wants me to start a GenAI company by the last page, and so far it tells me why, how to price and sell, and how to build with no server, but not how to form the company.

It is for people starting a company with agents, and the author says Gen Z and Gen X, but the examples are mostly experts in their forties and big company buyers. I am the Gen Z reader he wants, but only parts 6, 7 and 9, and chapters 18, 19 and 40, were for me.

Partly. The honesty helps: the notes saying prices are hypotheses (ch 20), the GDPR correction (ch 24) and placeholders that say they are placeholders (ch 22, 37). What hurts is that a lot of the proof is the author's own companies, RiskMandate and SG/Send, which I cannot check.

Chapter 1 and 2 with the 2018 history, chapter 3 with graphs, and chapter 4 with Wardley maps, because I did not see why I needed them to decide job or company. Chapter 17's code review company lost me too. RiskMandate was never defined where I met it in 19.

It drags in part 1 (ch 1 to 5) and in the middle chapters that retell the 2018 book first. It rushes where it matters most: ch 22 and 37 on forming a company are a few hundred words and say they are empty. Chapter 39 repeats 19, so it also drags there.

I would move part 9 (the hands-on chapters) to just after part 1, or interleave each hands-on chapter with the part it belongs to. I would merge 19 and 39, and 22 and 37, cut chapter 5 down to the pivot story, and move 8 and 28 to an appendix. I would put the job-or-company question in chapter 1.

The test in chapter 18 and 19, give it away then take it away and see if they miss it, plus the Stripe fee arithmetic (below about £5 the fixed fee is the price). I would send those two to my course friend. Chapter 38's credits table too.

The company chapters are empty, which is the book's whole promise. The history and the author's own products take up a lot of room. Chapter 29 on Portugal and chapter 34 on storyboards are about the book, not me.

A person, mostly. It is in the first person, tells stories with dates and has odd bits like the XZ aside and admitting stalled Leanpub books. But the notes to Dinis, the heavy citation of numbers and the repeated chapters feel like an agent assembled it.

No, not at this version. If the company chapters were real I would pay £9.99 for the ebook, maybe, and read the hands-on part on my phone. Paperback at £19.99 only if a friend says it works. It would have to say how to form a company and drop the repeats.
Fill the company-forming chapters, and open with the job-or-company question and a first afternoon of action instead of 2018.
Maybe a course friend who is also asking about starting something, and my mum, who has been inside her field for twenty years, for part 6 and chapter 17.
rating_why: A promise I want, but the chapters that keep it are empty, and too much of what I read was history, the author's companies and repeats.

decision.why: Not as it stands. If the company chapters existed and were as plain as 18 to 19, I would buy the ebook at £9.99 on a friend's say-so.

findings.what: The chapter that should make the reader a registered company says it is not written, and chapter 22 says the same. The book's objective, to start a company by the last page, cannot be met in this candidate. This is the reason I would not buy now.
findings.quote: By the end of this chapter you will have a company: registered, with a name, a country and a bank account.

findings.what: The hands-on pricing chapter repeats chapter 19 almost sentence for sentence, down to the same RiskMandate ladder, the same free-is-not-free argument and the same gym study. A reader who read 19 meets it twice and stops.
findings.quote: Neither answer is a marketing problem. If friendlies will not take it free, a bigger audience will not take it either.

findings.what: The first chapter spends its length on 2018, the two generations, a founder-age study and the name, before saying plainly what the reader will do. A reader on a phone gets the promise in the fourth section.
findings.quote: Eight years later they are entering the workforce for real, and a lot of them are not looking for a job.

findings.what: Prices, programmes and examples keep being the author's own companies, and the chapter admits there is no paid run yet and the prices are hypotheses. It reads as selling the author's products, not as advice a student can act on.
findings.quote: The plan is honest about where it stands: no paid run yet, and the prices are hypotheses to test with the first ten customers.

findings.what: The central company example is a code review business built on graphs and the author's own tools, for a reader who has just asked job or company. It is hard to tell whether it is advice or a pitch, and it is too big for a first company.
findings.quote: What the company sells is a review attached to a repository that keeps the layered graph current per commit and shows each change at every altitude.

findings.what: The actionable hands-on workflows with a promised result are in the second to last part, 30 to 40. A reader who wants to act today should meet that style first, not after 29 chapters of argument.
findings.quote: By the end of this chapter you will have a folder for every person you deal with, an agent that reads those folders and drafts for you, and six lines of rules that make it safe.

findings.what: Wardley maps, explorer, villager and town planner are taught before the reader has a reason to care, and the chapter tells you to find your centre of gravity first. It is the book's frame, but it is jargon for a reader who came with a job question.
findings.quote: Every dot is a claim. The positions are judgements, and the judgements are the argument.

findings.what: Telling the reader to read on paper with a pen sits oddly in a book people may read on a phone, and the chapter spends many words on history.
findings.quote: Read it on paper, with a pen.

recommendations: Write the company chapters (22 and 37) before the book is sold: UK steps, costs, a bank account, in plain steps, with a student example.
Merge 19 and 39 and the two company chapters so no reader meets the same point twice.
Open chapter 1 by answering job or company, in the reader's voice, and cut the 2018 history and the generations section to a page.
Move the hands-on chapters (30 to 40) up, next to the argument chapters they belong to, or put a hands-on route up front.
Define RiskMandate, SG/Send and sgit when first met, and use more examples from outside the author's companies.
Cut the Wardley and graph chapters (3, 4) down or move them after part 6, with the jargon explained in one plain line.
Move the notes to Dinis out of the sold text, and give a student-specific credits column in chapter 38.
